value.overview: The Strong-billed Woodcreeper is a large, powerful woodcreeper of humid forests in Middle and South America. It climbs tree trunks and large branches while probing bark and crevices with its unusually heavy bill. Its plumage is mostly brown, with a paler throat and patterned underparts that help separate it from some other woodcreepers. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of mountain forests, where it is most often encountered singly or in pairs.
value.classification: The Strong-billed Woodcreeper belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the woodcreeper subfamily Dendrocolaptinae. Its scientific name is Xiphocolaptes promeropirhynchus.
value.identification: This is one of the largest woodcreepers, with a long, stiff tail, broad wings, and a distinctly thick, wedge-shaped bill. The upperparts are dark brown, while the throat is usually buff or pale brown. The breast and belly show dark streaking, scaling, or barring, with plumage details varying among regional forms. It usually climbs upward along trunks and thick limbs, often keeping to shaded forest interiors. Its loud, ringing calls may reveal it before the bird is seen.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad range from southern Mexico through Central America and across northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, the resident subspecies X. p. costaricensis occurs mainly in the central highlands and other mountainous areas, extending into western Panama. It occupies humid montane evergreen forest, cloud forest, mature foothill forest, and sometimes adjacent forest edges or older second growth. Costa Rican records include elevated sites in Alajuela and other forested mountain regions.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration known. Individuals may make local movements according to elevation, weather, and food availability, but the species remains present year-round in suitable Costa Rican forests.
value.breeding: The Strong-billed Woodcreeper is believed to nest in natural cavities, holes in dead or living trees, or abandoned woodpecker nest sites. As in other woodcreepers, the nest is probably placed above the ground and contains a simple lining of plant material or other debris. Breeding information is limited in some parts of its range. In Costa Rica, nesting is associated with mature forest that provides large trees, cavities, and a stable supply of arthropod prey.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of arthropods, including beetles, ants, termites, caterpillars, and other insects, along with spiders and other small invertebrates. It forages on trunks, limbs, vines, moss, and epiphytes, using its strong bill to pry into bark and crevices. The species may follow army-ant swarms opportunistically, but it also searches independently and can join mixed-species forest feeding flocks.
value.behavior: The Strong-billed Woodcreeper is usually unobtrusive and spends much of its time climbing vertically along tree trunks. It often pauses to inspect bark before moving upward in short hops, then flies to another trunk or branch. Birds are commonly encountered alone or in pairs, although they may associate with mixed feeding flocks. Vocal activity can increase during the breeding season, and its resonant calls carry well through mountain forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
